SHAURYA BAJAJ, Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology, India
Bug fixing and code generation have been core research topics in software development industry for many years.
The recent explosive growth in Large Language Models has completely transformed these spaces, putting in
reach incredibly powerful tools for both. In this survey, 27 recent papers have been reviewed and split into
two groups: one dedicated to Automated Program Repair (APR) and LLM integration and the other to code
generation using LLMs. The first group consists of new methods for bug detection and repair, which include
locating semantic errors, security vulnerabilities, and runtime failure bugs. The place of LLMs in reducing
manual debugging efforts is emphasized in this work by APR toward context-aware fixes, with innovations
that boost accuracy and efficiency in automatic debugging. The second group dwells on code generation,
providing an overview of both general-purpose LLMs fine-tuned for programming and task-specific models.
It also presents methods to improve code generation, such as identifier-aware training, fine-tuning at the
instruction level, and incorporating semantic code structures. This survey work contrasts the methodologies
in APR and code generation to identify trends such as using LLMs, feedback loops to enable iterative code
improvement and open-source models. It also discusses the challenges of achieving functional correctness and
security and outlines future directions for research in LLM-based software development.

This survey provides a comprehensive overview of AI-powered advancements and methodologies in automated program repair (APR) and code generation. It is structured into two main sections: a review of recent techniques for bug identification and correction using LLMs, and a summary of LLM-based code generation.

**Key takeaways:**

* LLMs are transforming the landscape of software development, especially in automated program repair and intelligent code generation.
* APR and code generation are now critical research areas with significant potential to elevate software reliability and performance.
* The survey offers a deeper understanding of the strategies and challenges linked to these approaches, driving progress in intelligent software engineering.
* It highlights the role of feedback mechanisms and the value of open-source models in enabling continual refinement of generated code.

3.1 How have AI techniques, especially large language models (LLMs), improved

Automated Program Repair (APR) can be used to achieve a number of goals, one being how it
can be applied to fix security bugs through numerous approaches. Security bugs often arise from
vulnerabilities like buffer overflows, input validation issues, race conditions, or improper access
control. APR can be used to address these issues in different ways, depending on the type of bug,
the repair technique, and the tools used. Below are several ideas on how APR can be applied for
fixing security bugs:
3.1.1 Security Bugs.
(1) Template Based Patching: There are many Automatic Program Repair (APRs) tools that
use already existing templates to fix security vulnerabilities [18] [19]. For instance, they can
fix SQL injection and other types of bugs. Thus, the process is made faster when at least some
bugs are already fixed.
(2) Dynamic Analysis for Security Bugs: Methods like fuzzing and symbolic execution are
the reasons for security flaws that might have been unnoticed at the time of the execution of
the program [12]. Afterward, the tools can generate dummy patches which will be tested by
executing on various inputs. The results of the testing will then enable the patches and input
to co-evolve, thus, the fix for the problem will be improved [17] [25] [12].
(3) Search-Based APR for Security: Search-based methods are widely utilized in different
APR and debugging systems to create and confirm patches based on mutations of the initial
code [25]. These tools likewise act in the same way as the previous ones, where they output
a list of likely patches and then use different methods to search for the optimal patch that
meets the given conditions [17] [25].
(4) Specification-Guided APR for Security Protocols: The APR tools we looked at mostly
used fuzzing to verify the security of different internet protocols. This process was done by
obtaining precise grammar and specifications for the protocols [25]. Then the patches are
checked by applying them on different kinds of inputs and they are tested on the protocols
[17] [19] [25].
(5) Input Sanitization and Validation Patches: The problem of security vulnerabilities in
software may be due to the fact that there is no proper input validation or sanitization. Such
a situation can lead to problems such as injection attacks or data corruption. Automated
Program Repair (APR) tools can detect these flaws by checking how inputs are treated
and processed in the code. One approach is to detect the lack of sufficient input validation

6 Avinash Anand, Nishchay Yadav, Akshit Gupta, Shaurya Bajaj
Greybox Fuzzing [23], a testing approach where the fuzzer has partial insight into
the program’s internal architecture, blending both black-box and white-box techniques,
is among the key strategies. Its aim is to craft test inputs that efficiently expose bugs using
dynamic feedback from the program’s runtime behavior. This technique has been effective in discovering bugs often missed by conventional testing methods [25] [12].
(3) Search-Based APR for Semantic Bugs: Evolutionary algorithms support
search-based APR by exploring alternative fixes. The generated candidates are assessed
via test suites or specs to identify those that resolve semantic inconsistencies. This includes modifying portions of code, executing the variants, and selecting the optimal one. It is particularly effective for semantic errors without obvious bug patterns.
(4) Specification-Guided Repair: These systems utilize formal specifications to guide bug fixes for semantic issues [7] [19]. Relying on expected behavior models, this method ensures patches both resolve bugs and uphold the system’s intended functionality [25].
3.1.3 Syntactic Bugs.
(1) Pattern-Based Patching for Syntax: Syntactic bugs — involving violations of language rules or malformed structures — can be resolved through pattern-driven APR systems. These use predefined fixes based on common syntax error patterns. FixMiner is a notable tool that mines past commits to derive repair strategies [5].
(2) Grammar-Based Fuzzing: These tools create program inputs that respect language grammar, altering inputs via ASTs to preserve syntactic validity. This helps expose errors linked to malformed or incomplete code.
(3) Search-Based Techniques: Similar to their semantic application, these explore syntactic fixes by evaluating many code mutations, identifying those aligning with syntax rules and program logic.
3.2 What recent trends have emerged for using AI in APR tools?
Emerging Trends:
• Pre-trained Models: Widespread use of large pre-trained models like Codex and CodeT5.
• Transfer Learning: Models pre-trained on general corpora are being fine-tuned for specific repair tasks.
• Self-Supervised Learning: Enables training on unlabeled code repositories.
• Explainable AI: Adds interpretability to model outputs.
• Interactive Debugging: Incorporates human-in-the-loop mechanisms.
• Multi-modal Models: Integrate code, comments, and documentation for richer context.
Recent innovations in APR streamline AI and LLM integration into coding workflows. Key examples:
(1) Pre-trained Models: Models like GPT-4, trained on extensive code corpora, dominate bug-fixing performance [12].
(2) Neural Fault Localization: AI-driven analysis of properties like temporal logic helps pinpoint bugs. ASTs support program reasoning [18] [17] [25].
(3) Auto Test Generation: AI tools can autonomously generate test cases [17] [25], ensuring fix validity.
(4) Test Coverage Improvement: Enhances patch quality by ensuring modifications are covered, reducing overfitting [17] [25].
3.3 What challenges are being faced in APR right now?
Despite progress, APR tools face ongoing hurdles:
(1) Accuracy & Reliability: False positives/negatives still occur [23], necessitating human oversight.
(2) Context Sensitivity: APRs struggle with large codebases and interdependencies [18].
(3) Resource Overhead: High memory/compute costs may impact productivity [11].
Common Challenges:
• Generalization: Struggles with novel or domain-specific bugs.
• Scalability: Large systems remain hard to debug due to complex interactions.
• Context Understanding: Business logic and domain nuances may be misinterpreted.
• Security: Auto-generated patches might introduce or overlook vulnerabilities.
• Training Data Bias: Over-reliance on common patterns may miss edge cases.
• Overfitting: Benchmarked-trained models may not generalize well.
• Ethics: Copyright concerns arise from training on proprietary code.
4 How do modern debugging tools and benchmarks help evaluate the effectiveness of
bug-fixing methods? What are the common gaps or limitations in these tools?
Benchmarking is vital to evaluate APR tools and their scenarios. Many reviewed papers benchmarked against state-of-the-art tools to expand APR reliability.
4.1 Modern Debugging Tools
Modern debugging tools automate fault detection and repair. FuzzRepair [25] and AFLNet [12] use fuzzing plus repair to navigate complex input paths. These tools test patch robustness under varying conditions.
ML models like CoCoNuT, SequenceR, and Tufano19 [9] enable patch generation from learned patterns. Models like CodeBERT, GraphCodeBERT, and CugLM [14] leverage semantic embeddings for effective fixes. TreeBERT and T5 [14] support structural code understanding for logical consistency.
Evolutionary tools like ARJA-e and REWARDREPAIR [17] apply genetic algorithms to validate scalable patches. TBAR and Darjeeling [25] use template-based repair; Prophet predicts patch correctness probabilistically. Fix2Fit and CPR [25] verify contextual patch integration to avoid regressions. SAVER and DLFix [9] use semantic analysis to maintain system integrity post-repair.
Together, these tools ensure repair solutions are scalable, accurate, and applicable.
4.2 Modern Benchmark Tools
Benchmarks standardize bug-fix evaluation. HumanEval and MBPP [27][20] assess code generation quality; MBPP compares repairs across solutions. Fuzzing benchmarks like ProFuzzBench [12] and SCTBench [23] test vulnerability discovery and concurrency bug handling.
DebugBench [20] and VulnLoc [25] test LLM-based debugging and bug localization respectively. Defects4J [17][9][13] offers a rich real-world Java bug dataset. TransCoder [27] evaluates translation with bug testing. Benchmarks offer controlled environments to test robustness and quality.
4.3 Common Gaps and Limitations
Despite advancements, issues remain:
(1) Generalization: Limited benchmarks lead to overfitting. Tools like QFuzz may miss bugs due to incomplete fuzzing [19].
(2) Tool Bias: Popular tools/benchmarks like Defects4J dominate, skewing results. Datasets like CodeSearchNet may lack diversity [7].
(3) Non-Determinism: Tools like EVOREPAIR yield inconsistent results, leading to unreliable evaluations [17].
(4) Security Gaps: APR tools often fail on memory bugs or side-channels in C/C++ [9][12].
(5) Input Validation: Sanitization patches may miss edge cases [25]. Memory bug handling remains weak.
(6) Weak Metrics: Evaluation using limited test suites or simulated bugs distorts results [17].
(7) ML Limitations: Rare tokens and long patches remain difficult for ML models [9].
5 How do different AI models and tools compare in handling various code-related
tasks? What are the main strengths and weaknesses of these models?
This section compares models for code completion, bug repair, summarization, and translation. Codex [15], CodeT5 [21], GraphCodeBERT [6], WizardCoder [24], Magicoder [22], Mixtral [3], Smaug [16], Zephyr [4], DeepSeek-Coder [7], OpenCodeInterpreter [26], Phind [1], StarCoder2 [2], SPT Code [14], and GPT-4 are assessed.
Codex is real-time friendly but falters in complex scenarios. CodeT5 is great for localized codebases but lacks Codex's responsiveness. GraphCodeBERT captures dependencies well but is resource-heavy. Phind and DeepSeek-Coder excel in multilingual and mid-context tasks. StarCoder2 leads in HumanEval+ but struggles with C++. Smaug and Zephyr shine in accuracy but trail GPT-4 in logic reasoning.
For bug repair, Codex handles common bugs quickly but misses contextual issues. CodeT5 excels in precision but not speed. GraphCodeBERT is great for structure-sensitive bugs. Phind and DeepSeek-Coder perform reliably across logic-based tasks but falter in niche languages.
In summarization, CodeT5 and GraphCodeBERT provide structured and context-aware outputs. Codex is concise but less abstract. GPT-4 offers deep understanding but is slower. SPT Code is effective but lacks generalizability. StarCoder2 excels but has security concerns.
For translation, Codex handles basics well; GPT-4 excels in precision. CodeT5 and GraphCodeBERT are accurate but slower. Phind and DeepSeek support many languages but may miss edge syntax.
Multilingual capabilities: Mixtral and Phind outperform others. Smaug lags in non-English use. GPT-4 is powerful but compute-heavy. Overall, Codex is best for fast coding, GPT-4 for complex logic, and newer models offer niche strengths with resource trade-offs.

6 How do AI models trained on general language datasets, specialized code datasets, or
self-supervised learning approaches differ in their ability to handle code-related
tasks?
The effectiveness of AI models in handling code-related tasks depends significantly on their training methodology. Different models utilize distinct training techniques that impact their performance in areas like code generation, debugging, and semantic comprehension. While many language models are initially trained on broad datasets that give them general linguistic capabilities, others are tailored to specialized code datasets to enhance their programming skills. Additionally, some models incorporate self-supervised or bootstrapped learning strategies to refine their results, each offering unique advantages and limitations.
Models like Codex [15], CodeT5 [21], GraphCodeBERT [6], and Phind [1] are typically pre-trained on general language corpora. Codex, which powers GitHub Copilot and integrates with the OpenAI API, is a prominent example. It was fine-tuned from GPT models with 12 billion parameters and initially trained on natural language data, later adapted using public code from GitHub. This dual-phase training enables Codex to outperform GPT-3 and GPT-J on HumanEval benchmarks, particularly due to features like iterative problem-solving. However, it can struggle with consistent handling of variables in complex code scenarios involving intricate dependencies and control flows.
CodeT5 [21], using a unified encoder-decoder architecture, bridges programming and natural languages to improve code semantic understanding. By leveraging developer-defined identifiers, it enhances its ability to detect defects and translate code. Its bimodal learning strategy positions it as a top performer on tasks from the CodeXGLUE benchmark. However, its heavy reliance on identifier recovery might limit its ability to grasp deeper structural code relationships. GraphCodeBERT [6] expands this by incorporating data flow graphs to represent code semantics beyond token sequences. Pre-trained on the CodeSearchNet dataset, it excels in tasks like code search and clone detection, although it may falter with complex logic needing broader control flow understanding.
Phind [1] enhances the CodeLlama-34B model using a proprietary dataset of 80,000 structured programming problems and advanced training techniques such as DeepSpeed ZeRO 3 and Flash Attention 2. Its 73.8% HumanEval benchmark pass rate is attributed to rigorous dataset validation and decontamination.
In contrast, models like OpenCodeInterpreter [26], StarCoder2 [2], SPT Code [14], and Magicoder [22] are trained primarily on specialized coding datasets, making them more adept at programming tasks. OpenCodeInterpreter transforms filtered single-turn code queries into rich multi-turn dialogues, mimicking realistic human feedback. It learns from both correct and intentionally flawed code, improving its debugging prowess—especially effective for solving problems on platforms like LeetCode. StarCoder2 [2] fine-tuned on a vast programming corpus, translates text to code effectively and improves through interactive feedback.
SPT Code [14] focuses on encoding source code sequences for use in code completion and translation, using a two-stage process of pre-training and task-specific fine-tuning. Magicoder [22] utilizes OS code snippets through its OSS-INSTRUCT method to create high-quality instructions and outperforms many larger models despite its smaller size. However, it may inherit biases from its training seeds, leading to variable output quality.
Lastly, models like DeepSeek-Coder [7], WizardCoder [24], Mixtral [3], and Smaug [16] employ self-supervised or bootstrapped learning paired with innovative training methodologies. DeepSeek-Coder, fine-tuned for programming tasks on a large open-source corpus, applies instruction fine-tuning and Fill-In-the-Middle training to predict and complete code efficiently, even for long-form tasks, with its large 128K-token context window. WizardCoder [24] introduces the Evol-Instruct method to auto-generate complex instructions, reducing human effort and boosting performance on hard problems. Mixtral [3] uses a Sparse Mixture of Experts approach, activating only relevant subsets of its 47 billion parameters for each task, optimizing performance and resource usage.

from a teacher model to a student model to improve alignment with human preferences. This approach
facilitates zero-shot learning which enables the student model to generalize effectively and
perform well on unseen tasks. By collecting human feedback, Zephyr
adapts its behavior to be more interpretable which allows it to be used for various language tasks.
Overall, these diverse methods illustrate the continuous advancements in AI models for programming
tasks, driven by distinct training strategies that yield varying outcomes and model performance.
7 Conclusion
This paper presents a comprehensive overview of recent literature on the use of LLMs and AI in the domain of
automated program repair and code generation. It aims to summarize and compile the
latest research to support researchers in understanding the current developments in
AI-driven solutions for code-related tasks, their effective use cases, and the challenges being addressed in this domain.
Additionally, it includes comparisons of all the surveyed tools
to assist in identifying the most suitable open-source models for enhancing
other use cases that currently lack robust AI-based solutions.

This paper offers a detailed survey of AI-driven advancements and strategies in automated program repair and code generation. It examines various approaches and models, including LLMs, direct distillation, preference optimization, and code-specific transformers.

It outlines the limitations and distinctions of each method and presents a comparison of several open-source tools.

The conclusion emphasizes the fast-paced evolution of AI-based code repair technologies, noting that continuous innovation is shaping the development of more effective and adaptable tools.
